newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark warns of "silk curtain" danger for EU.
newsitem.headline: Denmark warns of "silk curtain" danger for EU.

text.p: Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen on Monday urged the European Union to invite all countries wishing to join the grouping to begin membership talks simultaneously and avoid a "silk curtain" making outsiders of some states.
Speaking at a hearing on EU expansion held by his Social Democrat party, Rasmussen said the admission issue was one of his government's highest priorities.
"The EU Commission will be making a mistake if it thinks of filtering out some of the applicant states in advance," he said.

"The commission should present reports that evaluate each country separately. None should be counted in or counted out beforehand. There should be no silk curtain coming down through Europe that keeps some countries out of the Union," he added.
A government source said Denmark realised that talks with the different countries would not end simultaneously but felt that a level starting-line was important.
A recent report by the independent Danish Institute of International Affairs took the same view.
"In this way one can avoid some of the countries suffering what German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel called 'the double rejection shock' from both the EU and NATO," it said.
Diplomats expect the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation at its July summit in Madrid to invite the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland to join, while other applicants must wait.

A two-day meeting of EU foreign ministers agreed in principle on Sunday to a plan for a standing conference of EU candidates, saying it wanted to make all hopefuls, whatever their readiness for membership, feel embraced by the EU project.

European Commission President Jacques Santer acknowledged at a news conference that some of the 10 eastern European countries queueing at the EU's door might not be deemed ready to start immediate entry talks when the Commission reports in July.
"Some...will find it easier to accede than others," he said, after ministers met in the Dutch country town of Apeldoorn.

Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Romania, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have all been promised eventual EU membership, but only a handful are seen as eligible at present.
